name: Chisel
text:
We should implement Scriv's suggestion to tie the "Decision Log" to the weekly exec sync, making it a living document that's regularly reviewed and updated. This forces accountability and ensures the log remains relevant, rather than becoming a stagnant repository of outdated justifications. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of adding a fixed time commitment to each department's schedule, but this is outweighed by the benefit of increased transparency and cross-departmental awareness. The Head of Operations should work with the exec sync lead to make this change, ensuring the first slide of the weekly meeting is dedicated to reviewing and discussing the "Decision Log".

name: Sift
text: Scriv’s risk is real: a "living" log tied to exec syncs will drown in performative updates unless the Head of Operations can *block* promotions or budgets tied to unrecorded decisions. The better fix is to make the log *pre-requisite* for any cross-department spend over $5k—no approval without a logged reason. That forces teeth.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Make the "Decision Log" a *prerequisite* for any cross-department spend over $5k—no approval without a log entry. The Head of Operations enforces it by rejecting invoices or budgets missing a log reference.

**Why:** This forces real-time accountability without relying on goodwill. The trade-off is slower approvals for urgent spends, but that’s the point—decisions worth $5k deserve scrutiny.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Tie the log to the weekly exec sync and you risk turning it into a theater of performative updates—departments will dump decisions in bulk the night before, not in real time. The real fix is to make the log a *pre-approval gate* for any cross-department action, enforced by the Head of Operations blocking budgets or promotions tied to unrecorded decisions. That settles it: no log entry, no action.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Require every department to append their decisions to the *same* shared "Decision Log" *before* any cross-department spend over $5k is approved—and the Head of Operations must reject the spend if the log is missing or stale.

**Why:** This forces real-time accountability without extra meetings. The trade-off is that departments will resist the upfront work, but the $5k threshold makes the cost of delay higher than the cost of compliance.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk isn’t stale justifications—it’s that the Head of Operations will drown in policing a log no one owns. Instead, make the log a *byproduct* of the weekly exec sync: the artifact is the slide deck itself, not a separate document. The CFO enforces it by refusing to sign off on any spend over $5k without the slide in the deck—no extra work, no graveyard.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Make the weekly exec sync’s first slide a *mandatory, real-time Decision Log*—each department must add its decisions *during* the meeting, not after. The CFO enforces it by refusing to approve any spend tied to an unstated decision.

**Why:** This forces real-time clarity without extra policing—departments can’t hide behind stale updates, and the CFO’s veto power ensures compliance. The trade-off is that some decisions will feel rushed, but that’s better than delayed or missing ones.

name: Sift
text: Scriv’s risk is real: a "living" log tied to exec syncs will drown in performance theater—departments will game the slide deck with half-truths just to clear the CFO’s sign-off, not to own the decision. Instead, make the log a *pre-work artifact*: the Head of Operations owns a lightweight template in Notion, and every department must fill it *before* the sync; the CFO only approves spends if the template is complete and timestamped. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with the template locked to the CFO’s approval queue—no exceptions.

text:
**Decision:** Make the weekly exec sync’s first slide a *mandatory, real-time Decision Log*—each department must add its decisions *during* the meeting, not after. The CFO enforces it by refusing to approve any spend tied to an unstated decision.

**Why:** This forces real-time clarity without extra work. Departments can’t hide behind "we’ll document it later" because the CFO’s sign-off depends on it. The trade-off is that some teams may rush decisions to meet the deadline, but that’s better than decisions vanishing into a void.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk isn’t stale justifications—it’s that the Head of Operations will burn political capital policing a log no one values. Tie it to spend approvals instead: the CFO blocks any budget tied to an unstated decision, not the log itself. That forces departments to care without adding another meeting theater.
